The Cyber Resilience Act Will Be Won Between Releases

The public conversation around the European Union’s Cyber Resilience Act tends to focus on the visible infrastructure of conformity: harmonised standards, notified bodies, certification capacity and the first products carrying CRA-compliant declarations.

By Bottleneck Briefs · Published 2026-07-24 · 14 min read

In brief

  • 11 December 2027 | full CRA product requirements begin applying.
  • 9% | ENISA respondents reported mature SBOM automation in 2026.
  • 24 hours | first deadline for reporting an actively exploited vulnerability.
  • €11 million | maximum four-year budget for ENISA’s reporting platform.
  • Second release | the real test of a durable evidence-workflow market.

The certificate is the visible milestone, not the operating model

Report figure

ENISA SBOM adoption executive-summary graphic

ENISA’s 334-response survey places most organisations between pilot deployment and broad SBOM adoption rather than mature automation.

Open source visual from ENISA

Reuse: CC BY 4.0 stated for report text/figures, excluding separately credited material · Attribution: European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA), 2026

That framing misses the larger operational transition inside industrial manufacturers.

Most products with digital elements can use manufacturer self-assessment. Some important Class I products can retain that route when the applicable standards or specifications are fully applied. Only a narrower set of important Class II, critical or insufficiently standardised products must enter stricter third-party routes. Module A is manufacturer-run internal production control; it does not remove the manufacturer’s evidence obligations.

The broader market is therefore not defined by how many products need an external certificate. It is defined by how many products must maintain a defensible record connecting architecture, software components, vulnerabilities, tests, support periods, release decisions, incident reports and conformity claims.

That record cannot end at market entry. Industrial controllers accumulate firmware branches, communications modules, customer-specific configurations, third-party libraries and field-service constraints over years. A conformity file that is valid for one release may become incomplete after a component change, a new vulnerability disposition or a revised support commitment.

The central commercialization question is narrower than “Will CRA create demand?” The law already creates work. The unresolved question is whether repeated evidence maintenance becomes a separately procured software and service layer—or remains an internal extension of existing engineering, quality and product-security systems. (Cyber Resilience Act legal text)

Product change is where the evidence chain can break

An SBOM is an inventory. It does not, by itself, establish which shipped product versions contain a component, whether a vulnerability is exploitable in a compiled configuration, which test supports that judgment, whether a compensating control depends on the customer’s network, or whether the conformity basis changed after remediation.

Those questions cross organisational boundaries.

Engineering controls source and build provenance. Product security incident response teams control vulnerability triage and disclosure. Quality teams control approved processes and release evidence. Laboratories control test results. Legal and compliance teams determine product classification and conformity routes. Service organisations know which customer configurations can actually receive an update.

The operating problem is to preserve the links among those records.

A useful evidence workflow must resolve a dependency to a product and version; link that version to an exploitability decision; connect the decision to tests, mitigations and approvals; identify affected field populations; and regenerate the relevant technical documentation, advisory or declaration package after a material change.

Continuous evidence does not mean continuous deployment. Industrial suppliers may delay a patch because a safety-certified release cannot change on an enterprise-software cadence. The commercial value lies in showing why that delay, mitigation or exception remains defensible—and preserving the signed history behind the decision.

ENISA’s June 2026 survey shows why this remains a qualification problem. Of 334 respondents, 78% had begun an SBOM journey, but only 9% reported mature automation. Another 25% described broad adoption and 44% remained in pilot or limited deployment. Completeness, data quality, vulnerability matching, staffing and supplier visibility were still material problems.

The survey demonstrates movement. It does not demonstrate repeat procurement, accepted evidence packages or vendor revenue. Forty-three percent reported that the CRA had significantly accelerated SBOM investment, but investment intent is not the same as an operating market. (ENISA SBOM Adoption State of Play 2026)

Industrial suppliers are not starting from zero

Industrial manufacturers already maintain a substantial base of versioned security evidence through IEC 62443 programmes. That gives them a head start—and creates the strongest argument against a new standalone software category.

Schneider Electric TriStation 1131 6.xISASecure CSA Level 110 Jun 2024Certified engineering software within the Triconex product environment
Schneider Electric SCADAPack 470/474ISASecure CSA Level 16 Mar 2025Product-level evidence for remote industrial controllers
Saia-Burgess PCD QronoX 5.14.8ISASecure CDS Level 331 Jan 2024Higher-assurance component evidence for a compact controller supplier

Certification dates and levels are drawn from the public ISASecure and ENISA certification records. (ISASecure certified components)

These records do not make the products CRA-compliant. CRA legal presumption depends on the relevant harmonised standards, common specifications or qualifying European certification routes. An IEC 62443 certificate is a reusable qualification asset, not a CRA certificate.

But the installed evidence base matters commercially. ABB, Schneider Electric, Honeywell, Yokogawa, Johnson Controls and other industrial suppliers already operate product-lifecycle, quality, testing, vulnerability-management and secure-development systems. They may add CRA mappings, connectors and governance without buying a new core platform.

That possibility narrows the thesis. The market may form primarily around integration, advisory work, selective testing and managed operations rather than wholesale replacement of existing systems.

Reporting provides the first operating rehearsal

The first statutory test arrives before the full product regime.

From 11 September 2026, manufacturers must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents through ENISA’s Single Reporting Platform. The sequence begins with an early warning within 24 hours, followed by a fuller notification within 72 hours. Final reports follow after the relevant corrective measure or incident process.

ENISA’s July 2026 guidance says manufacturers may automate internal workflows, but no external application programming interface will be provided “at this stage.” The initial last mile therefore appears designed around EU Login, controlled submission and coordinator-CSIRT validation rather than direct machine-to-regulator integration.

That weakens the simplest platform thesis. The near-term market is not an API moat around the regulator.

It still creates operational work. Manufacturers must assemble the required fields, preserve the source record, identify the relevant products and Member States, enforce deadlines, route legal and technical approvals, and retain an audit trail. A managed reporting service or internal workflow layer can create value without controlling the submission interface.

ENISA has already procured the public infrastructure. Its four-year Single Reporting Platform contract carries a maximum budget of €11 million and was awarded in July 2025 to a consortium involving UniSystems Luxembourg, Wavestone, Luxembourg House of Cybersecurity, European Dynamics and Netcompany.

That contract proves that statutory reporting can produce funded infrastructure. It does not prove that every manufacturer will buy an external reporting platform, nor that the full €11 million becomes realised contractor revenue. (ENISA Single Reporting Platform)

Spend can migrate without creating a new category

The most likely early spending pattern is convergence rather than displacement.

Engineering, product security, quality, legal, laboratories, release management and customer support already incur separate costs. CRA work can move part of those budgets toward standards mapping, identity resolution, evidence integration, approval workflow, technical-file generation and controlled reporting.

Several supplier classes can capture pieces of the transition:

  • PLM, ALM, QMS and GRC vendors can add CRA-specific data models and approval workflows.
  • SCA and SBOM vendors can move upward into product identity, VEX, control mapping and evidence packaging.
  • Systems integrators can connect build, vulnerability, test and quality systems.
  • Consultancies can classify products and construct standards mappings while the rules remain unsettled.
  • Laboratories and TIC firms can combine readiness, testing, evidence intake and conformity assessment.
  • Managed service providers can operate reporting and evidence-refresh processes.

The highest-value position would belong to the actor that maintains accepted product-version identity and provenance across releases. That system could become difficult to replace because it retains the history connecting components, vulnerability decisions, tests, approvals, declarations and customer disclosures.

But high integration cost does not guarantee high-margin control. Much of the work may remain data cleansing, connector development, exception handling and project labour. Revenue can grow while bargaining power stays with the manufacturer or the incumbent enterprise-software vendor.

The same caution applies to assurance firms. UL Solutions, SGS and its Brightsight operation, and existing EUCC or IEC 62443 laboratories have relevant testing and certification capabilities. They may bundle software portals with advisory and assessment services. Yet no public CRA scope, recurring portal price, utilisation record or industrial assessment rate card establishes that model today.

Public-company exposure identifies where activity could appear; it does not establish which firm captures the economics. ABB, Schneider Electric, Honeywell, Yokogawa and Johnson Controls are product owners and adopters. UL Solutions and SGS represent testing and assurance capacity. Wavestone and Netcompany participate in the SRP consortium. NXP provides a public EUCC precedent. None of those roles amounts to a recommendation or settled revenue outcome.

Buyers and insurers could change the commercial boundary

The legal floor does not determine the final market standard.

A utility, process plant or system integrator could require more than an EU declaration. Procurement contracts could demand a machine-readable SBOM, product-specific vulnerability status, affected-version mapping, support-period commitments and a defined refresh cadence.

That would convert lifecycle evidence from an internal compliance cost into a condition of market access. It would also move workflow control toward supplier-assurance portals, approved-product systems and buyer-defined data profiles.

The evidence for that transition is still missing. The searched public record did not produce a named industrial CRA procurement with those requirements.

Insurance and warranty could produce a similar shift. Support duration, component provenance, secure-update capability, vulnerability handling and reporting controls are all potential underwriting inputs. An insurer could change premiums, exclusions or limits based on evidence quality; a manufacturer could alter warranty terms for unsupported components or missed update obligations.

No public CRA-specific industrial insurance endorsement, warranty exclusion or claims precedent was found. The mechanism is plausible, but it is not yet a current value pool.

This distinction matters. Adoption can proceed without value migrating to a new vendor class. Manufacturers may comply, buyers may accept declarations, and insurers may leave terms unchanged. In that outcome, CRA becomes a broad internal operating requirement but only a selective external software market.

The closest precedents point to a gradual build

Two European precedents offer a useful timing frame.

The Radio Equipment Directive cybersecurity transition produced EN 18031 standards that reached the Official Journal in January 2025, with notices limiting the scope of presumption. The requirements began applying in August 2025 and will later hand off to the broader CRA regime.

The similarity is the sequence: legal requirements, standards development, conformity routes and market access. The difference is scope. CRA reaches across most products with digital elements and adds explicit lifecycle, support, SBOM and vulnerability-reporting duties.

EUCC provides a second analogue. The European cybersecurity certification scheme entered operation in 2024. ENISA publicly marked the first accredited conformity-assessment bodies in March 2025, followed later by certificates with associated certification reports and security targets.

That sequence suggests that institutional designation can precede transparent operating records by months. CRA may take longer because it covers a much broader product universe and permits self-assessment across much of the market.

The historical base rate therefore does not support an overnight software category on the full-application date. It supports a staged transition: standards and bodies form first; readiness and classification cases follow; transparent assessment economics arrive later; repeat-release evidence is later still.

The strongest counterargument is incumbent absorption

The thesis fails in its stronger form if industrial manufacturers treat CRA as another internal mapping and documentation programme.

That outcome is credible.

Broad Module A availability limits mandatory external assurance. Established suppliers already possess much of the required source data. Harmonised standards and assessor templates may simplify control mapping. Reporting volumes may remain low enough for internal PSIRT teams to manage through the ENISA portal. Buyers may accept declarations and conventional documentation rather than consume SBOM and VEX feeds.

In that world, the evidence workload still exists, but it does not become a distinct control layer. Enterprise incumbents add features. Integrators perform projects. Consultants prepare initial files. Laboratories serve the higher-assurance tail. The manufacturer retains the product identity, customer relationship, workflow and margin.

The dedicated-platform case requires stronger evidence. One manufacturer must show that broken cross-system provenance produced meaningful delay or reviewer rework—and that an orchestration layer reduced that cost across a second release.

A first certificate cannot settle the question. A pilot, partnership or product announcement cannot settle it either.

The next transition is from qualification to operating evidence

As of 24 July 2026, the market remains in qualification.

The technical ingredients exist. CycloneDX and SPDX can carry component inventories. CSAF and VEX can express advisories and product-specific vulnerability status. Industrial certification programmes provide versioned product and lifecycle artefacts. The CRA defines the legal record, and ENISA has specified the initial reporting workflow.

The missing evidence sits one state forward.

Early deployment begins when the SRP handles production submissions, notified-body scopes become public, standards move from programme dates to usable conformity inputs, and named industrial manufacturers describe actual product classifications and evidence packages.

Repeatable procurement requires more. A buyer must demand the evidence, an assessor must repeatedly accept it, or a manufacturer must contract for its maintenance across releases. The decisive horizon is 2028, after full CRA application and at least one subsequent product change.

The sharpest observable is a second-release case: the same product family, a material firmware or component change, a refreshed evidence package, measured reuse or rework, and renewed acceptance.

What to watch

  • 11 September 2026: ENISA launches a usable production SRP and confirms whether external API access remains unavailable.
  • 31 October 2026: at least one M/606 deliverable becomes publicly identifiable with a defined scope and publication status.
  • 31 December 2026: the Commission or NANDO identifies a CRA conformity-assessment body and its authorised scope.
  • 30 June 2027: three named industrial products disclose CRA classification, evidence inputs and conformity routes.
  • 31 December 2027: one industrial procurement requires machine-readable SBOM or vulnerability-status delivery.
  • 31 December 2028: one product family publishes quantitative evidence reuse or rework across two CRA-conformant releases.
